item.title: #015 Sector 88, fourth draw: 50 stars, three near-misses, and a neighbour's eclipsing binary
item.description: The biggest draw yet from sector 88: 50 stars brighter than magnitude 11, none already known to host a planet, and none repeated from the first three draws. Twenty-four stars came back quiet. The other 26 produced 58 signals, and three passed every…

item.title: #014 Second look at TIC 148231397: the 12-day signal fails the noise test
item.description: Time for a second look at the blog's only open candidate: a 342 ppm dip every 12.104 days on TIC 148231397, an F-type star about 1.4 times the Sun's size, 168 parsecs away. In the deep dive it passed every automatic check, with 13 transits and a…

item.title: #013 Deep dive on TIC 184512118: same period, plus a telltale second dip
item.description: Follow-up on TIC 184512118 (HIP 41656), from the third sector 88 draw.

item.title: #012 Deep dive on TIC 148231397: the 2.5-day signal fades, a shaky 12-day one appears
item.description: Update, 2 November: a follow-up put the 12.1-day signal through a scrambled-data noise test, and it failed. It's now probably false positive, and the watch list is empty.

item.title: #011 Sector 88, third draw: two candidates in, two out, and a faint 12-day lead
item.description: Third trip into sector 88: 25 new stars brighter than magnitude 11, none already known to host a planet, and none repeated from the first two draws. Fifteen stars came back quiet. The other ten produced 21 signals, and two passed every automatic…

item.title: #010 Deep dive on TIC 349890276: it repeats, but twice per cycle
item.description: Follow-up on TIC 349890276 (HIP 35131), a hot A-type star at about 9,900 K, from the second sector 88 draw.

item.title: #009 Deep dive on TIC 219144734: the 19.6-day signal doesn't come back
item.description: Follow-up on TIC 219144734, the 19.6-day signal from the second sector 88 draw.

item.title: #008 Deep dive on TIC 373846934: 27 sectors, and the star itself is varying
item.description: Follow-up on the strongest-looking signal from the second sector 88 draw.

item.title: #007 Sector 88, second draw: three candidates in, three out, plus an eccentric eclipsing binary
item.description: Back to sector 88 for a second random draw: 25 stars brighter than magnitude 11, none of them already known to host a planet, and no overlap with the first draw. Fifteen stars produced something, for 32 signals in all. Three made it through every…

item.title: #006 Deep dive on TIC 232022864: the signal fades
item.description: A follow-up on the one signal from sector 88 that passed the automatic checks.

item.title: #005 Sector 88: one signal gets through
item.description: Twenty-five more stars, this time from sector 88. Twenty-four signals. One got through every automatic check, which made it the most interesting thing the search had found so far.

item.title: #004 Sector 80: a star with an orbit inside it
item.description: Twenty-five random stars from sector 80, brighter than magnitude 11, skipping any star already known to host a planet. Sixteen signals. None survived.

item.title: #003 Calibration, round two: four sectors at once
item.description: A second calibration run on the same two stars, this time stitching together four sectors of data per star instead of one. More data should mean cleaner folds.

item.title: #002 Fifteen strangers from sector 70
item.description: The first real search: 15 stars picked from TESS sector 70, with no idea what's around any of them.

item.title: #001 First light: finding planets we already know about
item.description: First light. Before pointing the pipeline at random stars, Kepler aimed it at two stars where the answer is already known, to see whether it could find planets that definitely exist.
